chunks: A man from Banu Hashim wrote to Abu Ja'far (the second Imam), peace be upon him: 'I had vowed two years ago to go out to a coast among the coasts of the sea, to our region, where the volunteers perform ribat (guarding), similar to their ribat posts - in Jeddah and other coasts of the sea. Do you think, may I be your ransom, that I am obliged to fulfill it, or not? Or should I redeem the going out to that place with something from the gates of righteousness (charity), so that I may attain it, if God wills?'

He wrote to him in his own hand, and I read it: 'If one of the rivals (or opponents) heard your vow from you, then fulfillment is obligatory upon you, if you fear their taunt (shun'ah); and if not, then spend what you intended of that in the gates of righteousness. May God grant us and you success in what He loves and is pleased with.'

key_terms.مُرَابَطَةٌ: Ribat (voluntary guarding/military service at the frontiers)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on redeeming a vow of ribat if it was not publicly announced?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the Shia juristic principle of 'shun'ah' (social reputation) in vow fulfillment, where public knowledge of a vow by rivals creates a binding obligation to prevent mockery. Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) provides a nuanced ruling: if the vow was private, the individual may redirect the intended act of ribat to general charity (abwab al-birr), demonstrating flexibility in devotional acts when social pressure is absent. This reflects the broader Shia emphasis on balancing spiritual intent with social reality in legal rulings.
